message:
test(host): hand over the two-dispatcher race, with its assertions unverified

Test 1, build 1. Read the second paragraph before running it.

This drives both control loops at once -- a UDP session with control tunnelled over the media
socket, and a TCP session on its own port -- against one host with a helper that never answers,
which is the arrangement the budget lock and the helper cap exist for. It was written for V8.

Its assertions have NOT been executed in their current form. Earlier revisions ran and failed
twice, both times because the assertion was wrong rather than the product; the corrections are
untested because running them starts a listening host, and the user asked about exactly that
activity. It is committed anyway because the reviewer is running isolated sessions already and
asked for the coverage -- a starting point they can run once costs the user nothing extra,
whereas a file only I can see is worth nothing to anyone.

The trap that produced both failures, so nobody rediscovers it. The budget is SHARED between the
dispatchers. The UDP session fetches previews on its own, so by the time a TCP request arrives the
window is usually already in cooldown and the answer comes back in 0ms -- which is the shared
budget working, not a missed measurement. An assertion of the form "each side pays a deadline" is
wrong. The current ones check what is actually true: both sides are answered, each within one
deadline, and the pair costs less than two.

There was a third failure that was mine and is worth recording as a correction: when the UDP
session would not get a window list I suspected the TCP dispatcher was interfering with it.
Running the same session with --no-tcp failed identically. The cause was this test not passing an
encodedFrameSink, without which the session does not stay connected. Nothing to do with two
dispatchers, and nothing to do with the product.

Opt-in like its sibling: REMOTE60_ALLOW_HOST_E2E=1, otherwise it prints why it skipped and starts
nothing. Verified -- a default run leaves zero processes and opens no port.

What IS established, by my own measurement rather than inference: both dispatchers really do run at
once. A UDP client connecting makes the host log "client connected transport=udp" and then
"control waiting port=44761" -- the TCP listener does not exist until a media client has arrived,
which is also why this test connects the UDP side first.
